author: Subramanian J H

chapters.title: Foundations of CAE — Stress, Strain & Engineering Basics

topics.title: What is Stress and Strain?
concept: Stress is the internal force experienced by a material per unit area when subjected to an external load.
Strain is the deformation or displacement a material undergoes in response to that stress.
Stress (σ) = Force (F) / Area (A) → unit: Pascals (Pa) or N/m²
Strain (ε) = Change in Length / Original Length → dimensionless
why: Understanding stress and strain is foundational to all of FEA and CAE work. These concepts allow engineers to predict:
How material behaves under different loading conditions.
In FEA, stress and strain distributions help simulate real-world mechanical behavior without physical testing. This drives faster design cycles and improves safety margins.
usecases: When a side collision occurs, FEA simulations predict stress distribution to identify deformation zones. Strain data ensures doors absorb impact while protecting passengers.
Stress-strain behavior under cyclic loading helps in designing engine mounts that minimize vibration transmission while withstanding long-term fatigue.
everyday: As you stretch it, the force creates stress; the elongation you see is strain. Too much strain, and it snaps.
Your weight applies stress on the legs. If the chair bends slightly, that’s strain. Good design ensures the plastic doesn’t exceed safe stress/strain limits.
qa: Define stress and strain with units.
Stress = Force / Area (unit: Pascal); Strain = Deformation / Original Length (unitless).
What is the difference between true stress and engineering stress?
Engineering stress uses original area; true stress uses instantaneous area during deformation.
Why is strain unitless?
Because it’s a ratio of two lengths (no units).
In which case would strain be negative?
During compressive loading, the material shortens, resulting in negative strain.
How do stress and strain relate in elastic vs plastic regions?
In the elastic region, they are linearly related (Hooke’s Law). In the plastic region, strain increases without a proportional increase in stress.
Why do we need to study stress-strain before simulation?
It helps define material behavior and failure criteria for accurate FEA modeling.

topics.title: Hooke’s Law and Young’s Modulus
concept: Hooke’s Law states that within the elastic limit, the strain in a material is directly proportional to the applied stress.
E = Young’s Modulus, the proportionality constant (also called Modulus of Elasticity)
Young’s Modulus defines the stiffness of a material. A higher E means a stiffer material.
why: Hooke’s Law gives the basis for linear material behavior in FEA. Before a material yields or fractures, most metals behave elastically and obey this law. It simplifies simulations by enabling linear static analysis for small deformations.
It is used in stress calculations.
It helps choose materials based on stiffness requirements (e.g., steel vs rubber).
usecases: Designers use Young’s Modulus to control how much a spring compresses under load, balancing ride comfort with stiffness.
When choosing between high-strength steel or aluminum for doors or hoods, engineers compare their Young’s modulus to ensure structural integrity with lower weight.
everyday: When you pull a small elastic band lightly, it returns to shape – that’s elastic behavior, governed by Hooke’s Law. Pull it too far, it won’t recover – elastic limit breached.
If it bends or curves slightly under tension and springs back without deformation, it’s showing elastic behavior dictated by its material’s modulus.
qa: State Hooke’s Law and its equation.
Stress is proportional to strain within elastic limits: σ=E⋅ε
What does Young’s Modulus signify?
It measures material stiffness; higher modulus = more rigid.
Give examples of materials with high and low Young’s Modulus.
High: Steel (~200 GPa), Low: Rubber (~0.01 GPa)
Why is Young’s Modulus important in FEA?
It defines how much a material deforms under stress, directly affecting simulation accuracy.
Can Hooke’s Law be applied to plastic deformation?
No. Hooke’s Law only holds in the elastic region. Beyond yield, the relationship becomes nonlinear.

mcqs.q: Stress is defined as the internal force experienced by a material per unit of what quantity?
mcqs.exp: Stress equals force divided by area (σ = F/A), giving units of Pascals (N/m²).

mcqs.q: Why is strain a dimensionless quantity?
options: It is force divided by area
It is a ratio of two lengths
mcqs.exp: Strain is the change in length divided by original length, so the length units cancel out.

mcqs.q: Hooke's Law states that within the elastic limit, stress is:
options: Proportional to the square of strain
mcqs.exp: Hooke's Law gives σ = E·ε, meaning stress and strain are linearly (directly) proportional in the elastic range.

mcqs.q: In the equation σ = E·ε, a higher value of E indicates a material that is:
mcqs.exp: E is Young's Modulus; a higher E means a stiffer, more rigid material.

mcqs.q: Poisson's Ratio is defined as the negative ratio of:
mcqs.exp: Poisson's Ratio ν = −(lateral strain)/(axial strain), describing sideways contraction under axial loading.
